analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act entirely and replaces it with a different Republican health bill.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by one House Republican with zero cosponsors, was referred to eight committees and died in a subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the Affordable Care Act — the 2010 law that expanded health coverage, banned insurance companies from turning away sick people, and expanded Medicaid — as if it had never been passed. In its place it would enact a different bill, the OPTION Act of 2009, sponsored by the same congressman, that proposed a different approach to health insurance. The bill was referred to eight House committees on the day it was introduced, then sent to a Health subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would have been higher-income households, because the health care law pays for its coverage expansions partly through taxes that fall mostly on top earners and on parts of the health industry. People who preferred not to buy insurance or who disliked the law's requirements would also have been relieved of them. Health insurers would have been freed from the law's rules requiring them to cover people with pre-existing conditions, though they also would have lost the millions of new subsidized customers the law brought them.

how_it_helps.text: It would repeal both the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act and the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010, effective as if they had never been enacted, and restore the law as it stood before them [S2][S3].
It would enact the OPTION Act of 2009 (H.R. 3889, from October 2009) as a replacement framework [S2][S3].
Removing the law would have removed its financing, which relied in part on taxes on high earners and health-industry products — a real cost for those households and industries [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The people who would have borne the cost are those who gained from the health care law: uninsured people who would have lost access to subsidies and coverage expansions, people with pre-existing conditions who would again have been subject to insurance denials, seniors who would have lost the law's gradual closing of the Medicare prescription-drug coverage gap, and people who would have faced the return of lifetime coverage caps.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the law effective as of its enactment would have stripped coverage expansions, protections for people with pre-existing conditions, and the Medicare prescription-drug gap closure from tens of millions of people, without the replacement bill necessarily restoring equivalent guarantees [S2].

The bill acknowledged the real cost of the health care law in good faith: it required most people to carry insurance and financed its expansions with new taxes, and a good-faith opponent could argue those burdens fell on people who did not want or use the new coverage [S2].

The bill offered no transition or phase-out; it struck the entire law at once, which even critics of the law generally agreed would create immediate disruption for people already enrolled in new coverage [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core trade-off was straightforward: it would have ended the taxes and mandates of the 2010 health care law, but at the price of taking away the coverage expansions and consumer protections that same law provided. Because the replacement bill it pointed to was a broad framework rather than a point-by-point substitute for the law's specific guarantees, the net effect for people already relying on the law's coverage would likely have been a loss. The bill had no cosponsors, and no committee ever evaluated that trade-off in a hearing or markup.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to eight committees on the day it was introduced, then to a Health subcommittee, and it stayed there until the Congress ended — no hearing, no vote, nothing.

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Broun of Georgia introduced the bill on April 20, 2010, three weeks after the health care law was enacted [S1][S3].
No other House member signed on as a cosponsor [S4].

The bill was referred to eight committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and Labor, Appropriations, Judiciary, Natural Resources, House Administration, and Rules — the standard route for a bill touching many jurisdictions [S5].
On May 3, 2010, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, and no further action was ever recorded before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people who had gained coverage or protections under the 2010 health care law were better off, because the law remained in effect. The bill's sponsor gained a public record of opposing the law, which carried political value, but the bill never came close to becoming law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People keeping their ACA coverage and protections

for.name: Rep. Paul Broun (R-GA)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and issued no follow-up floor action; it was his only vehicle for full repeal with a replacement.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of primary referral; its Health Subcommittee received the bill
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the May 3 referral to the Health Subcommittee; no markup or hearing was held.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Republican and no Democrat or other Republican cosponsored the bill, so no vote ever tested where the parties stood; the Democratic House majority simply never acted on it.

industries.note: Repeal would have freed insurers from rules requiring them to cover people with pre-existing conditions and from other consumer protections, but it would also have stripped the law's subsidized customers and individual mandate from them. Their interest in shedding regulation ran against keeping coverage guarantees for ordinary people.

The 2010 law was financed in part through taxes falling mainly on top earners and investment income; repeal would have removed those. The saving for this group would have come at the cost of the law's coverage expansions.

industries.industry: Health industry sectors subject to the law's taxes and fees
industries.note: Parts of the health industry faced new fees and taxes under the 2010 law to help finance coverage expansions; repeal would have lifted those. The trade-off for the public would have been losing the expansions those payments helped fund.
